«God dag,» sagde troldet; «er Smørbuk hjemme idag?»
“Good day,” said the troll; “is Smørbuk at home today?”

20438.etyen:
Fixed greeting formed from god (“good”) + dag (“day”), literally “good day”.
God (“good”) is from Old Norse góðr (“good”), from Proto-Germanic *gōdaz (“good”), ultimately from Proto-Indo-European *gʰedʰ- (“to join, unite, suit”). Dag (“day”) is from Old Norse dagr (“day”), from Proto-Germanic *dagaz (“day”). The further origin of the latter is uncertain.
Compare the parallel formations Norwegian Nynorsk god dag, Danish god dag, Swedish god dag, Faroese góðan dag and Icelandic góðan dag (“good day”).

Kamerun thus became a German protectorate from 1884 to 1919 — in practice an authoritarian German colony.

1000406.etyen:
Internationalism, ultimately from Portuguese Camarões (“Cameroon”), after Portuguese Rio dos Camarões (River of Shrimps), an early name for the present-day Wouri River, given because of the abundance of shrimp in the river. The name contains the plural of camarão (“shrimp, prawn”), from Latin cammārus (“lobster”), with Portuguese -ão (“augmentative suffix”), ultimately from Ancient Greek κάμμαρος (kámmaros, “a kind of lobster or shrimp”), from Pre-Greek. The further origin is unknown. The immediate donor of the Norwegian form is unknown.
Parallel international adaptations include Norwegian Nyn

1001942.etyen:

Compare Danish Johannessen, Faroese Johannessen, Swedish Johannesson and Icelandic Jóhannesson (“patronymic surname”).
